last_assistant_message: Computer terminals evolved from simple telegraph-based teletypes in the 1960s into specialized devices for interacting with mainframe computers, initially using paper-based input and output before transitioning to cathode-ray tube (CRT) displays in the 1970s. Video display terminals (VDTs) became the standard interface for business and scientific computing, allowing users to send commands and receive instant visual feedback rather than waiting for printed results. The personal computer revolution of the 1980s and 1990s gradually displaced dedicated terminals, as individual workstations could now serve the same purpose with greater flexibility and computing power. Despite this shift, terminal emulation software preserved the terminal interface as an essential tool for system administrators, programmers, and power users who valued its efficiency and direct access to operating systems. Today, command-line terminals remain central to software development, server management, and Unix-like systems, representing a remarkable continuity of interface design that has persisted for over 60 years despite massive changes in underlying hardware technology.
